parts.note: morse is an old name for the walrus
L is the usual abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A walrus wanders off holding a mouthful of food.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse is an archaic word for the walrus, from the same root as the Russian name for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small bite or piece of food, exactly what fits into one bite.

parts.note: surface reading: pictures that have been skilfully made
setter's reading: brought up from a well, as petroleum is, so the paintings are named after what comes out of the ground

explanation.walkthrough: Well-produced sounds like praise for craftsmanship, but the well is an oil well.
explanation.definitionFit: Pictures done in oil paint are called by the medium's name, and that medium is pumped up from wells.

clue.text: Combination of wind and frost causes a pile-up in winter

indicators.note: a combination mixes things together, so the letters of the two words are blended into a new order

parts.note: the two weather words supply the letters; and only joins them

explanation.surface: Wintry wind and frost together cause a traffic pile-up on the roads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pile-up' suggests a road accident, but here it is a heap of snow; 'and' is just part of the fodder's joining.
explanation.definitionFit: Wind heaps falling snow into banks, so a snowdrift is literally a heap of snow seen in cold months.

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the name is only one possible arrangement of its letters

parts.note: the man's name supplies all six letters

explanation.surface: A host is asked to present someone called Daniel to the company.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead in is to bring something in first or usher a person into a room, much like presenting or starting things off.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the central wedge stone locking an arch in place
second meaning: the bumbling cops of the silent film comedies made by that studio

explanation.surface: Someone is the chief backer of a troupe of funny policemen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch-supporter' reads like 'chief fan'; it is literally what holds up an arch. The Keystone Kops were slapstick police in early Hollywood silent films.
explanation.definitionFit: The top central stone holds an arch together, and the Keystone studio's slapstick police films gave the second meaning.

clue.text: Stole points inside, so won easily

indicators.note: inside says one word sits within the other, splitting the phrase for theft around it

parts.note: knocked off is slang for stole
spots are the pips or points on dice and cards

explanation.surface: A cheat pocketed points during the game and so won without effort.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-word slang phrase for stealing is split, with the second word of the answer placed between its parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To knock spots off a rival is a British idiom for beating them comprehensively and with ease.

clue.text: Andy's one to provide a non-committal answer

indicators.note: to provide is to make up or produce, so these letters are worked up into a new phrase

parts.note: every letter of the name with its 's and the number word

explanation.surface: Andy is the person who can be relied on to give an evasive reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is unusually faint: only 'provide' tells you the preceding letters are to be reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying both yes and no commits to neither side, the classic hedged reply to a question.

indicators.note: making means forming something new, so the word's letters are made into another word

parts.note: taken as the letters to rework

explanation.surface: An instruction to begin baking some pastries.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarts are open pastry cases with sweet or savoury fillings, a common kind of baked pastry.

clue.text: It's not often the present combines with the past

parts.note: the present moment is now
and is the word that joins or combines
then refers to a time gone by

explanation.surface: A musing that the present and the past seldom come together.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning occasionally, at irregular intervals, which describes something that happens infrequently.

clue.text: Place represented as loaded with gold

indicators.note: something represented is shown in a different form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A place is portrayed as being stuffed with gold.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is gold in heraldry, a standard crossword source. The surface is nearly a definition itself, since the fabled city was said to be full of gold.
explanation.definitionFit: El Dorado is the legendary South American city of riches that explorers sought, a mythical location.

clue.text: Lie, in an open sort of way

definitions.text: Lie, in an open sort of way

parts.words: Lie, in an open sort of way
parts.note: surface reading: tell an untruth quite brazenly
setter's reading: recline, stretched out with limbs spread wide

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie' and 'open' point to a frank fib; it is lying down with arms and legs spread.
explanation.definitionFit: To sprawl is to stretch out loosely with limbs flung wide, so the body lies in an untidy, spread posture.

parts.note: surface reading: a cheerful, sociable atmosphere
setter's reading: a tune, one sung by merry companions over their glasses

explanation.walkthrough: 'An air of' usually means an atmosphere; here air is a melody.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a tune is sung in pubs and at parties by people sharing drinks, the very picture of jolly companionship.

clue.text: Worker in biblical community went to America

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the ship that made the voyage

indicators.note: in places the worker within the name of the place

parts.note: Samaria is the region and city of the Bible, home of the Good Samaritan's people
the worker ant is a crossword staple

explanation.surface: A labourer from a Bible-era town emigrated to the New World.
explanation.walkthrough: Samaria was the biblical capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. The definition is loose: it describes the vessel by what it did rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Santa Maria was the flagship of Columbus on his 1492 voyage across the Atlantic to the Americas.

clue.text: Wise men having a different image out East

indicators.note: different means changed, so the remaining letters are put in a new order
out means removed, so the compass letter is taken away

parts.note: taken as written
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Sages from the East picture things differently.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the E from IMAGE, then rearrange IMAG. The surface nods to the Magi coming from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: The Magi are the three learned astrologers of the Nativity story, traditionally called the Three Wise Men.

clue.text: Many diet perhaps, but it could result in a big blow-out

definitions.text: it could result in a big blow-out

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words are only one possible arrangement of their letters

parts.note: both words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Lots of people go on diets, yet a huge feast might follow.
explanation.walkthrough: A blow-out is British slang for a big meal, which fits the diet story; here it is a literal explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: This explosive is used for blasting rock, so it produces a large explosion that blows things apart.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: perform a shift, as a driver does with the gear lever
second meaning: a stopgap arrangement used until something better arrives

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is whimsical: split the answer and you get an instruction to effect a gear shift.
explanation.definitionFit: A makeshift is a stopgap expedient, something improvised to serve for now until a proper solution appears.

clue.text: Arrange to see her in Oxford, perhaps

indicators.note: to arrange is to put things in order, so these letters are set out afresh

parts.note: all three words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Someone plans to meet a woman in the university city of Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford looks like the city, but an Oxford is a laced leather shoe, and this goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe tree is a foot-shaped form put inside footwear to keep its shape, and an Oxford is one kind of lace-up.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a frame or con, British slang
second meaning: to sew closed a tear, so the rip gets smaller

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid to a landlord; here it is a tear in cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A stitch-up is British slang for a con or setup, and stitching up a rip mends torn fabric by sewing.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: hold back or retain
second meaning: the strongest central tower of a castle

explanation.surface: Someone is held for their own protection somewhere secure.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep a person is to hold them back, and a castle's keep is its fortified inner stronghold and last refuge.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the conquistador Keats called stout in his sonnet on Chapman's Homer
second meaning: the legislature of Spain

explanation.surface: A portly man sits among Spain's lawmakers.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's line 'like stout Cortez' refers to the conqueror of Mexico, usually spelt with a z there; 'stout' meant bold, not fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Hernán Cortés was the Spanish conquistador, and the Cortes Generales is the national legislature in Madrid.

parts.note: surface reading: an argument where both parties are justified
setter's reading: a right hand, so each side of the body is as skilful as a right hand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' suggests justice in a dispute; it is the right hand, treated as though one were on each arm.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who uses either hand equally well is as deft with the left as the right, as if having two right hands.

clue.text: It has a small part in a big picture

definitions.text: It has a small part in a big picture

parts.words: It has a small part in a big picture
parts.note: surface reading: a bit-part actor in a major film

parts.words: small part in a big picture
parts.note: setter's reading: a small panel set into a larger illustration or map

explanation.walkthrough: 'Small part in a big picture' sounds like an extra in a blockbuster; it is a small image placed within a larger one.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a smaller map or illustration set within the border of a larger one, often in a corner.

indicators.note: sound tells us the word is heard, not spelt, when said out loud

parts.note: to heal is to cure

explanation.surface: A dependable remedy for hypocritical talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound cure' reads as a reliable remedy and 'cant' as insincere talk; cant here means tilt, as a ship heels over.
explanation.definitionFit: Cant and heel both mean to lean or tilt to one side, as a vessel does in the wind.

clue.text: When used between rulers, it eliminates mistakes

indicators.note: between places one word in the gap separating the two rulers

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen; two rulers give two of them
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Something placed between drawing rulers on a desk rubs out errors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rulers' looks like stationery sitting next to the rubber; it is two monarchs, each ER.
explanation.definitionFit: An eraser is a rubber that removes pencil marks, so it gets rid of written errors.

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: all three words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Someone climbed into bed while intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got into' reads as one verb, but 'Got' alone is the definition and 'into a bed' the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain is to acquire or come by, which is what got means in a sentence like 'got a ticket'.

parts.note: an old salt is an experienced sailor
to beef is slang for to complain

explanation.surface: A seaman complains about the cured rations on board.
explanation.definitionFit: Salt beef is brisket cured in brine, a traditional way of keeping it edible for long periods.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: resolve or determine a matter
second meaning: come to rest and stay put, as a bird does on a branch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not to go on' sounds like quitting; it means stopping somewhere to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle a question is to resolve it, and to settle somewhere is to come to rest and remain there.
